judge_input.advisory_text:
This configuration creates a single Cloud Storage bucket in the US multi-region using the Standard storage class, plus an IAM binding that makes its objects publicly readable. The critical finding is that public read grant on google_storage_bucket_iam_member.public_read, and the bucket also lacks lifecycle rules, autoclass and versioning, so data that is never read stays in the most expensive storage class indefinitely. Cost is modest (about $2/month) and is driven entirely by the assumed volume of Standard-class objects, with operations and egress not yet counted.
google_storage_bucket.assets: The bucket has no lifecycle rule, so objects that stop being accessed remain in Standard storage, the class with the highest storage price, forever. Add a lifecycle rule that moves objects to a colder class (for example Nearline after 30 days or Coldline after 90 days) or deletes temporary/old objects, so unused data stops being billed at Standard rates.
google_storage_bucket.assets: Neither autoclass nor lifecycle rules are configured, so the bucket keeps everything in Standard even though the access pattern of the assets is unknown. If the access pattern is genuinely mixed or unknown, enable autoclass on the bucket so objects move to colder classes automatically and back to Standard when read; if the pattern is predictable, prefer explicit lifecycle rules instead, since autoclass adds a per-object management fee.
google_storage_bucket.assets: The bucket is located in the US multi-region, which is priced above a single region, while the configuration does not indicate a cross-region availability requirement. Suggestion (no documentation source): If assets are only served from one area, move the bucket to a single region (for example us-central1) to reduce the per-GB storage price; keep the multi-region only if you need the higher availability it provides.
judge_context: Autoclass: When to choose it over lifecycle rules. Autoclass fits buckets where the access pattern is unknown or mixed, because it needs no rules and has no retrieval fees or early deletion charges for the transitions it makes. It adds a management fee per object, so it is less attractive for buckets with a very large number of small objects. When the access pattern is predictable, explicit lifecycle rules are usually cheaper.

Autoclass: What it does. Autoclass moves each object between storage classes automatically, based on how that object is accessed. Objects that are not read move to colder classes over time, and an object that is read again moves back to Standard. It is enabled per bucket.

Object Lifecycle Management: What it does. Object Lifecycle Management applies rules to the objects in a bucket automatically. A rule has a condition, such as object age, number of newer versions or creation date, and an action, such as Delete or SetStorageClass. Typical rules move objects to Nearline or Coldline after 30 or 90 days, or delete temporary files and old noncurrent versions.

Object Lifecycle Management: Why it saves money. Without lifecycle rules, data that nobody reads stays in Standard storage forever. Moving old objects to a colder class or deleting them lowers the monthly storage bill without any application change. Rules are evaluated asynchronously, so an action can take up to a day to apply after an object meets the condition.

Storage classes: The four classes. Cloud Storage offers Standard, Nearline, Coldline and Archive storage. Standard has the highest storage price and no retrieval fee, and suits frequently accessed data. Nearline is cheaper to store and suits data read about once a month or less. Coldline suits data read about once a quarter. Archive is the cheapest to store and suits data read less than once a year.

judge_input.advisory_text:
This configuration creates a single n2-standard-4 web VM in us-central1-a with a 50 GB pd-ssd boot disk, plus two firewall rules. The most serious problem is a critical firewall exposure on the SSH rule (GCE-001), with additional high findings on the database firewall rule and the instance itself, so this setup should not be applied as-is. The entire $150.29/month estimate comes from the one VM, driven mainly by the N2 machine type and the SSD boot disk.
google_compute_instance.web: The VM uses an N2 machine type, which costs more than the E2 family for workloads like a web server that don't need N2's higher per-core performance. Switch to the equivalent E2 machine type (e.g. e2-standard-4) of the same vCPU and memory size to lower the compute price without changing capacity.
google_compute_instance.web: The machine type appears to have been chosen without measuring actual CPU and memory usage, which often leaves VMs oversized. Enable Compute Engine rightsizing recommendations and, before the infrastructure exists, start with a modest machine type and scale up after measuring real usage.
google_compute_instance.web: A dedicated VM for a web service requires OS patching, firewall management and manual scaling that a managed platform handles for you. If the workload is a stateless HTTP application or API in a container, consider moving it to Cloud Run, which provides an HTTPS endpoint, scales to zero and bills only for resources used while handling requests.
google_compute_instance.web: The boot disk is provisioned as pd-ssd, the most expensive per-GB type, but a stateless web server boot disk rarely needs SSD-level IOPS. Change the boot disk type from pd-ssd to pd-balanced; disks can be grown later without downtime, so you can start small.
judge_context: General-purpose machine families: E2 compared with N2 and N1. E2 machine types are the lowest-cost general-purpose family and suit web servers, small databases, development environments and other workloads without special CPU needs. N2 and N2D offer higher and more consistent per-core performance and larger shapes at a higher price. N1 is an older generation that is rarely the best value for new workloads.

General-purpose machine families: Shared-core types. The e2-micro, e2-small and e2-medium shared-core types are the cheapest option and suit small or bursty workloads that do not need a full vCPU all the time. Moving a workload that does not need N2 performance to an E2 type of the same size lowers its price without changing its vCPU or memory.

Machine type (rightsizing) recommendations: What they are. Compute Engine analyses the CPU and memory usage of each VM and recommends a machine type that fits it better. A VM that uses little of its capacity gets a recommendation for a smaller type with an estimated saving. A VM that runs hot gets a recommendation for a larger type.

Machine type (rightsizing) recommendations: How to act on them. Rightsizing is often the largest and safest saving, because many VMs are sized by guesswork. Before the infrastructure exists, choose a modest machine type and scale up after measuring. Custom machine types let you set vCPUs and memory separately when no predefined shape fits. Changing a machine type requires stopping the VM.

Persistent Disk types: Choosing for cost. You pay for provisioned size, not for used space, so oversized disks waste money every month. A boot disk for a stateless web or application server rarely needs pd-ssd: pd-balanced gives similar behaviour for much less. Keep pd-ssd for data disks that need high IOPS. Disks can be grown later without downtime, so start small.

Persistent Disk types: The disk types. Persistent Disk has several types. Standard (pd-standard) uses hard disk drives, is the cheapest per GB, and suits sequential or rarely accessed data. Balanced (pd-balanced) uses SSD and balances price and performance for most workloads. SSD (pd-ssd) costs the most per GB and is meant for databases and other latency-sensitive workloads.

Spot VMs: What they are. Spot VMs use spare Compute Engine capacity at a much lower price than standard VMs, with discounts that can be very large. In exchange, Compute Engine can stop (preempt) them at any time with short notice, and they have no availability guarantee. Spot VMs replace the older preemptible VMs and have no maximum runtime.

Spot VMs: Good and bad fits. Spot VMs suit fault-tolerant work: batch jobs, CI runners, data processing, stateless workers behind a queue and development environments. They are a poor fit for a single VM that serves users, or for databases, because the VM can disappear at any moment. Managed instance groups can recreate preempted Spot VMs automatically when capacity returns.

What is Cloud Run: When it is the simpler choice. A stateless HTTP application or API in a container usually runs on Cloud Run with far less to operate than a VM or a Kubernetes cluster: no operating system patching, no node pools and no cluster fee. Kubernetes Engine is the better fit when the workload needs Kubernetes APIs, custom networking, stateful sets or daemon sets. A small web service on a dedicated VM or a small GKE cluster is often a candidate for moving to Cloud Run.

What is Cloud Run: What it is. Cloud Run is a managed platform that runs containers without any servers or clusters to manage. A service gets an HTTPS endpoint, scales automatically with traffic, including down to zero, and is billed for the resources used while handling requests. Cloud Run jobs run containers to completion for batch work.

The entire estimated $39.42/month comes from keeping the minimum instances warm while idle, since request-based traffic is not included in the estimate.
google_cloud_run_v2_service.api: min_instance_count is set to 2, so two instances are kept warm and billed at the idle rate around the clock even when the service receives no traffic; this is the sole driver of the $39.42/month estimate. Lower template.scaling.min_instance_count from 2 to 1 (or to 0 if the service is not latency-sensitive, such as an internal tool or dev environment) so you only pay for the warmth you actually need.
google_cloud_run_v2_service.api: Each warm instance is allocated 2 vCPU while idle, which doubles the idle cost compared with a single-vCPU instance for a service whose traffic profile is unknown. Suggestion (no documentation source): Reduce template.containers.resources.limits.cpu from 2 to 1 and measure latency and throughput before considering a larger allocation; scale out with max_instance_count instead of over-provisioning each instance.
judge_context: Minimum instances for Cloud Run: What minimum instances do. By default Cloud Run scales to zero when a service receives no requests, and the next request waits for a cold start. Setting a minimum number of instances keeps that many instances warm so requests are served without that delay.

Minimum instances for Cloud Run: Cost. Warm instances are billed even when they handle no traffic, at a lower idle rate when request-based billing is used. A service with minimum instances therefore has a fixed monthly cost, while a service that scales to zero costs nothing when idle. Use minimum instances only for latency-sensitive services, and keep the value at zero for internal tools, batch triggers and development environments.

Cloud Run billing settings: Which to choose. Request-based billing is cheaper for services with low or uneven traffic. Instance-based billing can be cheaper for services with steady, high traffic, and is required for work that continues after the response is sent, such as background tasks. Combining instance-based billing with minimum instances means paying the full rate around the clock, so check that the workload really needs it.

Cloud Run billing settings: Two billing modes. With request-based billing, the default, CPU is allocated and billed only while an instance is processing requests, and there is a per-request fee. With instance-based billing, CPU is always allocated for the whole life of each instance, there is no per-request fee, and the per-second rates for CPU and memory are lower.

judge_context: IAP TCP forwarding for SSH and RDP: Firewall rule to use. Instead of allowing port 22 or 3389 from 0.0.0.0/0, allow them only from the IAP range 35.235.240.0/20. SSH and RDP ports open to the internet are scanned constantly and are a common way into a project. With IAP, access is tied to a Google identity and is logged, and the VM does not need an external address at all.

IAP TCP forwarding for SSH and RDP: What it does. Identity-Aware Proxy (IAP) TCP forwarding lets administrators reach SSH, RDP and other TCP ports on VMs that have no public IP address. The connection is wrapped in HTTPS and is allowed only after IAM checks that the user has the IAP-secured Tunnel User role.

IP addresses for VMs: Recommendation and cost. Most VMs do not need an external address. Serve user traffic through a load balancer, reach machines for administration through IAP, and send outbound traffic through Cloud NAT. External IPv4 addresses are billed, including static addresses that are reserved but not attached, so removing unneeded addresses reduces both exposure and cost.

Before the infrastructure exists, choose a modest machine type and scale up after measuring. Custom machine types let you set vCPUs and memory separately when no predefined shape fits. Changing a machine type requires stopping the VM.

Spot VMs: Good and bad fits. Spot VMs suit fault-tolerant work: batch jobs, CI runners, data processing, stateless workers behind a queue and development environments. They are a poor fit for a single VM that serves users, or for databases, because the VM can disappear at any moment. Managed instance groups can recreate preempted Spot VMs automatically when capacity returns.

Spot VMs: What they are. Spot VMs use spare Compute Engine capacity at a much lower price than standard VMs, with discounts that can be very large. In exchange, Compute Engine can stop (preempt) them at any time with short notice, and they have no availability guarantee. Spot VMs replace the older preemptible VMs and have no maximum runtime.

judge_context: GKE cluster fee and choosing a mode of operation: Fixed costs to remember. Every cluster has a cluster management fee charged per hour, in both modes, in addition to the compute it uses. A regional cluster runs its nodes in several zones, so a node count of 1 per zone means three nodes. For a few small services, one shared cluster, or Cloud Run with no cluster at all, is often simpler and cheaper than a dedicated cluster per application or environment.

GKE cluster fee and choosing a mode of operation: Standard and Autopilot. GKE has two modes. In Standard mode you create and manage node pools and pay for every node, used or not. In Autopilot mode Google manages the nodes and you pay for pod requests. Autopilot is the recommended default, and Standard is for cases that need specific node configuration or control.

GKE cluster autoscaler: What it does. The cluster autoscaler changes the number of nodes in a node pool to match what the workloads need. It adds nodes when pods cannot be scheduled for lack of capacity, and removes nodes that are underused when their pods can run elsewhere. You set a minimum and a maximum size per node pool.

GKE cluster autoscaler: Why it saves money. A node pool with a fixed node count is sized for peak load and is paid for all day. With autoscaling the pool shrinks when demand is low. It works on resource requests, so pods need realistic CPU and memory requests. Combine it with the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler so the number of pods also follows the load.

GKE Autopilot overview: What Autopilot is. Autopilot is a GKE mode in which Google manages the nodes, scaling, upgrades and security configuration. You deploy workloads and Google provisions capacity for them. Autopilot applies many hardening settings by default, including Workload Identity Federation for GKE and Shielded GKE Nodes.

GKE Autopilot overview: Cost model. In Autopilot you pay for the CPU, memory and storage that your pods request, not for whole nodes. Idle node capacity and system overhead are not billed to you, so Autopilot is usually cheaper for small or variable workloads and for teams that would otherwise leave nodes partly empty. Large, steady, tightly packed workloads can be cheaper on Standard mode, where you pay per node.

Idle node capacity and system overhead are not billed to you, so Autopilot is usually cheaper for small or variable workloads and for teams that would otherwise leave nodes partly empty. Large, steady, tightly packed workloads can be cheaper on Standard mode, where you pay per node.
